name: The Continuous Close
title: The Continuous Close
answer: The continuous close is the practice of keeping a company's books close to final at all times rather than treating month end as a single scramble. Instead of a batch of reconciliations, accruals and adjustments landing in the last few days of the period, those tasks are spread across the month as transactions occur. The aim is a set of accounts that is always substantially ready, so the formal close becomes a review and a sign off rather than a rebuild. It sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where the ledger, the subledgers and the reporting layer have to agree with each other continuously.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: The continuous close is the practice of keeping a company's books close to final at all times rather than treating month end as a single scramble. Instead of a batch of reconciliations, accruals and adjustments landing in the last few days of the period, those tasks are spread across the month as transactions occur. The aim is a set of accounts that is always substantially ready, so the formal close becomes a review and a sign off rather than a rebuild. It sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where the ledger, the subledgers and the reporting layer have to agree with each other continuously.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: It runs on an ERP or general ledger as the system of record, fed by bank feeds, payment processors, expense tools and billing systems that post through interfaces rather than spreadsheets. A reconciliation or close management layer sits on top, holding the matching rules, the task list and the audit trail. Data has to arrive on a predictable schedule, which usually means automated feeds and a defined cut off for each source. Where a source cannot be automated, the process still needs a named owner and a date, because an unreconciled feed is the main thing that breaks the always ready state.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is a mix of rules, matching and review. Bank and ledger lines are matched automatically on amount, date and reference, with exceptions routed to a person. Accruals and prepayments are generated from contract and invoice data on a schedule, and recurring journals post themselves. Machine learning is used mainly at the edges, to suggest a match, classify a transaction or flag an unusual pattern, while the posting decision stays with a controller. The close checklist becomes a live dashboard of what is done, what is waiting and what is blocked, and the period end is a checkpoint on that list rather than the start of the work.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because the books are always near final, the controls have to run continuously too. Each automated match and generated journal needs a traceable source, a rule or model version and a reviewer where materiality requires one. Segregation of duties still applies, so the person who configures a matching rule is not the only person who can post its output. Access to the close dashboard and to the adjustment log is restricted and logged. Provenance matters more, not less, when entries appear without a human keystroke, and auditors will ask how a balance was produced and who approved the rule behind it.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward fewer manual journals and more exception based review, with controllers spending their time on judgement rather than matching. That shift depends on clean source data and on rules that are maintained as the business changes, since an automated close built on stale mappings drifts quietly out of agreement. Adoption is uneven, and many finance teams run a hybrid where some entities close continuously and others do not. The open questions are how much of the close can be trusted without a person in the loop, and how audit and internal control adapt when the period end is no longer the moment the work happens.
